# Introduction
Blocked cluster randomized controlled trials (CRTs) are a widely used experimental evaluation design in which entire groups (clusters) such as schools or classrooms are randomly assigned to treatment or control conditions within defined strata or blocks. The effectiveness of the program or treatment is then typically quantified using the average treatment effect (ATE). However, within this relatively straightforward quantity, researchers must make a variety of choices. Researchers need to decide whether to target a person-weighted average or cluster-weighted average; they need to decide whether they are targeting an estimate just for the clusters in the study (finite sample) or an estimate representative of some broader population (superpopulation); and they need to decide from among different methods or estimators that can be used to estimate the ATE.

This paper contains simulations that complement research examining empirically the implications of different choices researchers make when performing CRTs (Miratrix et al., 2025). Simulations, unlike empirical analyses, allow us to compare estimated quantities to their true values, which we cannot observe in empirical contexts. This in turn allows us to evaluate how well different statistical methods perform. Additionally, we can systematically vary data conditions and identify which factors impact method performance.

# Research Questions

With this in mind, these simulations answer the following research questions:

1. Are any of the estimators ever substantially biased? When?
2. Are any of the estimators generally more precise than others? When?
3. Are any of the standard error estimators inaccurately calibrated? When?
4. Do any of the estimated standard errors target finite versus super-population uncertainty?
5. Why does the range in the estimates produced by the different estimators get larger as the degrees of freedom get smaller? Is the cause estimator bias or estimator instability?

# The Simulation

We ran a series of multifactor simulations, which are simulations where we systematically vary a set of factors to understand how the factors influence the performance of the various estimators, and how the factors interact with each other.
In general we are close to full multi-factorial designs, where we vary all factors independently, but we do drop combinations that do not make sense (in particular, we drop scenarios that call for correlations between quantities that do not vary).

One of our factors is "block type," which is a set of seven parameters that define how similar or different the blocks are from each other.
We did not independently vary these factors so we could control the total number of simulation scenarios.
All code is public; others can easily adapt the code to run additional scenarios that are of interest.
We have three levels of block type, which we call "Blocks All The Same," "Blocks All Reasonable," and "Blocks All Messy."
The "Same" case is where all blocks are identical in their characteristics.
The "Reasonable" case is what we might imagine we would see in actual practice.
The "Messy" case pushes our simulation to the limits so we can see how various methods fail in extreme circumstance.

# Data Generating Process

For most of our simulations, for each scenario defined by sample size, target correlation, predictiveness of covariates, and so forth, we used the following data generating process (DGP):

1. Randomly generate a single set of blocks based on the simulation scenario parameters. Each generated block has a set of characteristics such as the average treatment effect of the block, average cluster size, amount of cluster variation, and so forth.

2. Then, for each simulation iteration:
   a. Generate a sample of clusters within each block according to the block characteristics.
   b. Generate individual-level data within each cluster.
   c. Calculate the true ATEs (both cluster-weighted and individual-weighted) for the generated dataset. These are our target finite-sample estimands.
   d. Assign a proportion of clusters to treatment according to the target block-level proportion.
   
At this point we have a complete set of generated data.
Next, for each simulation iteration we actually conduct a small number of iterations. For each iteration we:

  a. Permute treatment across clusters within block to generate a new random assignment.
  b. Calculate observed outcomes based on the generated data and the new treatment assignment.
  c. Estimate the ATE and SE using all our methods.

The nested permutation approach means that for each fixed set of clusters and blocks, we can calculate finite sample performance.
For example, the standard deviation of the ATE estimates within a given dataset across the permutations gives us the true finite sample standard error for that dataset.
If we look at the standard deviation of the ATE estimates across all our datasets within a scenario, we have the true cluster-level superpopulation standard error.
This standard error _does not_ take into account uncertainty at the block level, as the block characteristics are all fixed.
So, for example, if there is treatment variation across blocks, our true standard error will not reflect uncertainty due to which blocks were generated, only uncertainty due to which clusters and individuals were generated.

For our target estimands we can use, within each generated dataset, the finite sample estimand.
We can also calculate the superpopulation estimand (both person-weighted and cluster-weighted) by averaging the finite sample estimands across all generated datasets within a scenario.


We next outline the data generation parameters that drive our DGP, and then give some further technical detail of how we implemented the above steps.




## How the data are generated

For a given scenario, we start with a set of data generating parameters as described above.

Here is one of the more extreme scenarios from our main simulation:

```{r}
scenarios = readRDS( here::here( "scenarios.rds" ) )

strp <- scenarios %>%
  dplyr::select( -grid ) %>%
  select(where(~ n_distinct(.x) > 1))

strp2 <- strp %>%
  filter( sd.cluster != 0,
          blocktype == "messy",
          p.bar == 0.7,
          J.bar == 10,
          cv.block != 0,
          cv.cluster != 0.6,
          sd.block != 0,
          num.cov.cluster == 5,
          size.intercept.cor != 0,
          ICC.cluster != 0,
          cv.cluster != 0,
          size.impact.cor.cluster != 0,
          size.impact.cor != 0 
          )
#strp2

key_ID <- strp2$ID
key_scen <- filter( scenarios, ID == key_ID )

key_scen %>%
  dplyr::select( -ID, -blocktype, -grid, -group,
                 -num.cov.block ) %>%
    mutate(across(everything(), as.character)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by( variable ) %>%
  summarise( value = paste( sort( unique( value ) ), collapse=", " ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable( caption = "Simulation Scenario Parameters" )
```


Then, to generate the individual blocks, we use a multivariate normal distributions to generate the block-level pairs of average control-side outcome and average treatment effect (in the case of treatment variation).
Other block characteristics that are to vary across block (e.g., proportion of clusters treated) are then generated according to various specified distributions.
Finally, we induce correlations between block level quantities as described below, if the relevant correlation parameters are nonzero.

When generating block mean outcomes and mean effects, we use the "empirical" setting to make sure our multivariate normal distributions for the amount of cross-block impact variation and so forth equals our set values.
This mitigates worry that the simulation results might be dependent on _which_ blocks we have generated, as we would expect all sets generated, given a specific set of parameters, would lead to the similar final results.
That said, we generate these values to target _block averages_, but if we have variable numbers of clusters per block, the cluster-average effects can deviate from these targets quite substantially, especially if number of clusters and treatment effect are correlated.

Overall, however, the finite nature of the blocks should not be a large concern.
In particular, because we have a large number of factors in our experiment, when we look at the main effect of a given factor, we will be averaging across many different scenarios with a different specific set of blocks for each scenario, so any dependencies on the specific set of blocks generated would be ameliorated.

Once generated, we store the block characteristics as a small dataset, which we call a "grid," with each row being a block, and each column a characteristic we need for generating the within-block data (number of clusters, average cluster size, etc.).
To illustrate, here is the "grid" of block-level characteristics for the above scenario in our main simulation:

```{r}
gd <- key_scen$grid[[1]]

#names(gd) <- str_replace( names(gd), "cluster", "clu" )
rename( gd,
        tau = block.tau,
        alpha = block.alpha,
        cor.clu = size.impact.cor.cluster,
        k.clu = num.cov.cluster,
        k.indiv = num.cov.indiv ) %>% select(-sd.cluster, ICC.cluster, R2.cluster) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits=1 )

```

and here is a set of descriptive features for data we would get from this fixed set of blocks:

```{r describe_scenario, cache=TRUE}
source( here::here( "R/data_generation_code.R" ) )
describe_block_grid( gd )
```

The block ATE is the simple average of the block-level cluster-average ATEs. It is as we targeted.
The bottom line are ATEs for a large dataset generated for this set of blocks: these are our approximated target superpopulation parameters for this scenario.

In this specific example, these are different from each other and from the block average.
We also see fairly high correlations of all sorts of features of the data. The numbers in parentheses are the standard deviations of a given value.

Given our grid of block characteristics we then, for each block in turn, use a multilevel model data generating process (as described more fully in Miratrix et al.,2021) to generate the target number of clusters and individuals.

To keep everything in effect size units, we have a target within-block total variation of $1 - ICC_3$, where $ICC_3$ is the target intraclass correlation for the blocks.
Note that we have $ICC_3 + ICC_2 + \frac{\sigma^2_\epsilon}{(1-R^2_1)} = 1$, with $ICC_2$ being the cluster-level ICC and $\sigma^2_\epsilon$ the individual-level residual variance.


## How we correlate block-level quantities

Given two vectors of numbers, $x$ and $y$, that we wish to correlate with target correlation $\rho$, we do the following:

1. Generate a bivariate standard normal with correlation $\rho$.
2. Re-order the $y$ values so the pairs of the ranks of $x$ and the ranks of the reordered $y$ correspond to the pairs of ranks of the bivariate distribution.

If $x$ and $y$ are not normal, then this will not produce correlations that have the target correlation on average, but it will generally give high correlations when $\rho$ is high, and negative correlations when $\rho$ is negative.
We are correlating based on the normal transform of the ranks, so this is somewhat akin to a rank correlation.

If we have multiple correlations, then we do these in sequence, holding one of the variables as fixed so we do not undo any of the other correlations.
For example, say we need to generate a scenario with both a correlation between the number of clusters in a block and average impact in the block, and a correlation of proportion treated in a block and average impact in the block.
To do this, we first generate the three vectors of number of clusters, average impact, and proportion treated.
We then rearrange, as described above, the number of clusters so it correlates with average impact, and next rearrange the proportion of clusters treated so it correlates with average impact.
This will induce a correlation between number of clusters in a block and proportion treated in a block, because they are both correlated with the block-level ATE.


## How we generate distributions of sizes

We have three kinds of sizes to generate: number of clusters per block, number of individuals per cluster, and average size of cluster for each block.

For each of these we use a similar approach.
We first specify the desired mean and coefficient of variation (cv).
For example, we might want an average of 8 clusters per block with a cv of 0.75.
This means the standard deviation of our values would be $sd = cv * mean = 0.75 * 8 = 6$.

We then have three possibilities: either the variance is less than the mean, in which case we can use a binomial distribution, or the variance is larger than the mean, in which case we can use a negative binomial distribution.
If the variance is very close to the mean, we use a poisson distribution.

We use this approach for the average cluster size across blocks, even though the average cluster sizes could be fractional.


# How to read the box plots in this paper
In this report, we use a set of boxplots customized for our particular data. Below is a sample boxplot of the mean bias of an estimator relative to its target estimand across simulation runs for all methods and scenarios. The faint horizontal lines extend to the full range of the data. The bars mark the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles, capturing 95% of the data. The boxes span the 10th and 90th percentiles, corresponding to the middle 80% of the data. Overall, the estimators exhibited negligible bias across a broad set of simulation conditions.


```{r readplot, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.width=5, fig.height=1.75, dpi=150}

sruns.graph.bias<-sruns.clean  %>% 
  filter(method %in% core.methods) %>% 
  mutate(method = str_remove(method, "-db$"),     
         method_ordered = str_remove(method_ordered, "-db$"))

fig1cap<-"Figure 1: Sample boxplot for paper. This boxplot shows the superpopulation mean bias of each estimator relative to its target estimand across scenarios and methods. The faint horizontal lines extend to the full range, the bars span the 2.5th to 97.5th percentiles, and the boxes span the 10th to 90th percentiles."


# First create the base plot
bias_plot_full <- create_custom_boxplot3(
  sruns.graph.bias %>% filter(group == "fullfactor"), 
  "bias.s.estimand", 
  "", 
  "Super Population Mean Bias Against Targeted Estimand",
  vline_at = 0
)


# Calculate the percentiles from your data to position the labels
data_for_percentiles <- sruns.graph.bias %>% 
  filter(group == "fullfactor") %>% 
  pull(bias.s.estimand)

percentile_values <- quantile(data_for_percentiles, 
                              probs = c(0, 0.025, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.975, 1))

an_size = 3.0
alt_pos = 1.4

bias_plot_full <- bias_plot_full +
  # Add percentile labels
  annotate("text", x = alt_pos, y = percentile_values["0%"] - .005, 
           label = "Min", size = an_size, hjust = 0.5, family = "serif") +
  annotate("text", x = alt_pos, y = percentile_values["2.5%"], 
           label = "2.5%", size = an_size, hjust = 0.5, family = "serif") +
  annotate("text", x = alt_pos, y = percentile_values["10%"]+.012, 
           label = "10%", size = an_size, hjust = 0.5, family = "serif") +
  annotate("text", x = alt_pos, y = percentile_values["90%"] + 0.005, 
           label = "90%", size = an_size, hjust = 1, family = "serif") +
  annotate("text", x = alt_pos, y = percentile_values["97.5%"], 
           label = "97.5%", size = an_size, hjust = 0.5, family = "serif") +
  annotate("text", x = alt_pos, y = percentile_values["100%"], 
           label = "Max", size = an_size, hjust = 0.5, family = "serif") +
  # Add your theme
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(-0.25, 0.25, by = 0.03)) +
theme_minimal() +
theme(
  text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 10),
  axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8, family = "serif"),  # This is the horizontal axis with values
  axis.text.y = element_blank(),  # This hides the "1" on the vertical axis
  axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),  # Also hide the tick marks
  plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 12, family = "serif"),
  plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 9, family = "serif", color = "gray40"),
  legend.text = element_text(size = 9, family = "serif"),
  legend.title = element_text(size = 10, family = "serif"),
  panel.grid = element_blank()
)

# Then create your final plot with caption
ggdraw() +
  draw_plot(bias_plot_full, 0, 0.1, 1, 0.9) +
  draw_label(
    str_wrap(fig1cap, width = 110),
    x = 0.05, y = 0.05,
    hjust = 0, vjust = .5,
    size = 9, color = "gray40", fontfamily = "serif"
  )




```
# Are any of the estimators ever substantially biased? When? 

Before diving into the results we note that the aggregation regression estimators are identical (in terms of point estimate) to the individual regression estimators as we did not include level 1 covariates in this simulation, so we present bias results for 7 core estimators that produce different point estimates.

Overall, the magnitude of bias was less than 0.01 for at least 80% of the simulation scenarios tested for all estimators (Figure 2).
That said, we do see evidence of bias larger than this under some circumstances for several different methods.


We only see any degree of bias under a confluence of multiple bias-causing factors (Figure 3).

First, the estimators that theory predicts are essentially unbiased indeed do not appear to have bias (or possible have very low bias) across the full range of simulations.

In some of the simulations, the person-weighted fully interacted estimator (LR-FIpw) is predicated to have a bias with a magnitude of as large as .03, which the regression tree shows requires a correlation between the treatment effect and cluster size combined with a small number of clusters per block, large cluster size variation, and unbalanced treatment assignment (Figure 3).
Overall it is a stable performer with little potential for bias.

For the remaining estimators, except the multilevel fully interacted model, we observe bias as severe as -0.2 in some simulations, primarily driven by the combination of messy blocks and unbalanced treatment assignment of clusters.
The magnitude here is large, but it is important to note here that the messy block condition was deliberately designed to push parameters to the extreme.
In particular, the messy block condition has a 0.8 correlation between the proportion of each block assigned to treatment and the block-level treatment effect, which is particularly problematic for the multilevel estimators because it shifts the estimator weighting from cluster to person.
Our simulations do not show substantial bias under the data generating conditions we expect to see in practice (i.e. for the same and reasonable block type conditions).

Finally, the multilevel fully interacted model performed well even with messy blocks and unbalanced treatment assignment.
It's vulnerability is driven by a combination of correlation between the number of clusters and the treatment effect, zero cluster-level ICC, and substantial variation in cluster size.
This causes the estimator to lean more person-weighted (due to the zero ICC), which is considered bias when the estimator is viewed as targeting the cluster-weighted estimand.

```{r biastree, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=6,dpi=150, results='asis'}
# Simple faceted analysis trees
methods <- setdiff( sort( unique(sruns.graph.bias$method) ), "LRcw-FIcw" )


fig3cap <- "Figure 3: Regression tree by method predicting the magnitude of the mean bias under different data generating parameters" 

# Set up plotting layout
par(mfrow = c(3, 2), oma = c(3, 0, 0, 0))

for (method_name in methods) {
  create_analysis_tree(
    sruns.graph.bias %>% filter(method == method_name, group == "fullfactor"), 
    outcome_var = "bias.s.estimand.mag", 
    predictor_vars = c("block_type", "J.bar", "cor_J_tau", "sd.clu", "ICC.clu",
```

# Are any of the estimators generally more precise than others? When? 

In general, all the different estimators have comparable precision (Figure 4). Excluding the multilevel estimators, within a given scenario, all the estimators have standard errors that are at most 10% larger than the median across methods. The multilevel estimators become more precise than the other estimators when there is a combination of large variation in cluster size and zero cluster ICC; otherwise, their precision is close to that of the other estimators (Figure 5).

# Which estimators have calibrated estimates of the treatment effect standard error?

Overall, across scenarios, the standard error estimates for fully interacted estimators, except the fully interacted MLM, are too small relative to the true super population standard errors (Figure 6). However, across almost all simulations, the magnitude of the underestimate estimate is very small. The only exception is the fully interacted CRVE estimators in some simulations produced severely underestimated standard errors. These were all simulation conditions that likely produced blocks without at least one treated and one control cluster, or where either all the treatment or control clusters will be very small (Figure 7). This is part of a broader caveat, which is that almost all the fully interacted estimators are undefined in cases where there are only two clusters in any block. While, the fully interacted CRVE estimators do have defined standard error estimates in these cases, the low degrees of freedom simulations confirmed that these estimates are extremely poor and these estimators should not be used under these circumstances.

On the other hand, the estimated standard errors for the other estimators are on average systematically too high across the simulations. For the MLM, the amount of overestimation is small except when there is a confluence of an unbalanced sample, zero cluster-level ICC, and cross-cluster treatment effect variance (Figure 8). 

For the fixed effect estimators, the standard errors are well estimated in the same and reasonable blocks conditions. However, we find the standard errors were poorly estimated in the messy blocks, especially when there was no cluster-level ICC were the standard errors are predicted to be overestimated by at least 15% (Figure 9). Although again it is important to remember that the messy blocks condition was designed to test when the estimators break and are not conditions we expect to see in practice. Within these scenarios (i.e. messy blocks and no cluster level ICC), the person weighted estimates were even more overestimated, with this overestimation problem mostly getting worse the less variation there was across clusters. 

Consistent with the standard errors being generally well estimated across simulation conditions and estimators, the coverage rate is close to 95% across simulation conditions and estimators (Figure 9). For the MLM models, coverage could fall below 90% under some conditions (e.g., no variation in cluster size, no cluster-level ICC, and at least three other factors) (Figure 10). Under these conditions the weighting for the MLM models shifts from being cluster weighted to person weighted, which causes these estimators to be biased against the cluster weighted estimand; which in turn causes the coverage rate to drop. For the CRVE estimators, the coverage drops predictable under the same conditions that the standard error estimates get worse. Otherwise, there were generally no issues with confidence interval coverage.

# Do any of the estimated standard errors target finite versus super population uncertainty? 

The simulations demonstrate that the standard errors are targeting the super-population standard errors (with blocks being fixed, clusters being sampled for block specific superpop). The true super-population standard errors are only noticeably different from the true finite population standard errors when the cluster-level ICC is zero and there is cross-cluster treatment effect variance (Figure 11). Looking at the subset of simulations where that is true shows that the standard error inflation is consistently closer to one for the true super-population standard errors than for the true finite population standard errors (Figure 12).

```{r finiteexplore, include=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
                                                 "cv.clu", "num.cov", "p.bar"),
                            tree_title = "Decision Tree for Ratio of Estimated SE over True Finite SE")

fin_plot6 <- create_custom_boxplot2(
  sruns.clean %>% filter(group=="fullfactor" & (ICC.cluster==0 & sd.cluster=="+" & is_pw==T & is_FI==T & J.bar=="S"& cv.cluster=="L" & block_type=="Mess")) ,  
  "inflate.s", 
  "Super Population Estimated Standard Error Accuracy by Method", 
  "Ratio of Estimated SE over True Super SE",
  vline_at=1,
    log_scale = TRUE
) + theme(legend.position = "none")

fin_plot7 <- create_custom_boxplot2(
  sruns.clean %>% filter(group=="fullfactor" & (ICC.cluster==0 & sd.cluster=="+" & is_pw==T & is_FI==T& J.bar=="S" & cv.cluster=="L" & block_type=="Mess")) ,  
  "inflate.f", 
  "Super Population Estimated Standard Error Accuracy by Method",

  vline_at=1,

fin_plot6 + fin_plot7 + plot_layout(widths = c(2, 3))
```

# Why does the range in the estimates produced by the different estimators get larger as the degrees of freedom get smaller? Is the cause estimator bias or estimator instability?

In the empirical studies the range of estimates produced by different estimators was larger for the low degrees of freedoms studies. Simulations show that this is because the estimates get are more unstable when the degrees of freedom is smaller and not because of anything to do with estimate bias. In the simulations as the degrees of freedom get smaller, the estimate instability gets larger (Figure 13). On the other hand, we see no relationship between mean bias and degrees of freedom in a given scenario (Figure 14).


\begin{table}[H]

\hline
\multicolumn{3}{|c|}{\textbf{Cluster Weighted}} \\
\hline
Multi-Level Model & 

Bias can exceed .04 in simulations when there was a combination of correlation between the number of clusters and the treatment effect, zero cluster-level ICC, and  a lot of variation in cluster size \newline

In the non-fully interacted MLM models, bias also can exceed .04 when there are messy blocks.  \newline

Bias variation trade off because the multilevel estimators become more precise than the other estimators when there is a combination of large variation in cluster size and zero cluster ICCs & The standard errors were substantially overestimated in simulations with a confluence of an unbalanced sample, zero cluster-level ICC, and cross-cluster treatment effect variance \\
\hline
Fully Interacted & Minimal bias under all conditions & Except CRVE, very small under estimate of the standard errors under all conditions \newline
CRVE standard errors are poorly estimated with a small number of clusters and an unbalanced sample \newline

Can not be used if any of the blocks only have two clusters \\
\hline
Fixed Effect & Bias can exceed .05 in simulations when there is a combination of messy block and unbalanced proportion of treated and control clusters & Standard errors were substantially overestimated for messy blocks and no cluster-level ICC\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
